key_facts: Infestation of the scalp hair by the louse ***Pediculus humanus capitis***.
Very common in children aged **4–14**; spread by **head-to-head contact** (lice crawl, they cannot jump or fly).
Diagnose only by finding a **live louse** with wet or dry **detection combing**; nits alone do not prove active infestation.
Options: **wet combing** (bug busting) or a physically acting product such as **dimeticone 4%**, repeated after 7 days.
Check all household members and treat only those with live lice; children need not miss school.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: Head lice are scalp infestations with *Pediculus humanus capitis*, a wingless blood-feeding insect about 2–3 mm long. They are commonest in **children aged about 4–11**, especially girls. They are **not a sign of poor hygiene** and do not transmit disease in the UK.

sub: Worldwide, all social groups; commonest in primary-school children, more often **girls** (longer hair, closer contact).
Direct head-to-head contact; sharing brushes or hats is a minor route.

ul: Spread is by **direct head-to-head contact**. Lice crawl; they cannot jump, fly or swim. Hats and brushes rarely matter because lice die within about 1–2 days off the scalp.
Females glue eggs near the scalp. Eggs hatch in about 7–10 days; adults live about 3–4 weeks on the host.
**Nits** are empty white egg cases that move out as hair grows. Nits far from the scalp usually mean an old infestation.
Itch may take **4–6 weeks** to appear at first infestation; many children never itch.
Risk factors: female sex, more children in the family, sharing beds, combs and hats.
Resistance to older insecticides (permethrin, malathion) is widespread, so physical or mechanical methods are preferred.
**"Lice mean dirty hair"**: lice prefer clean or dirty hair equally.
**"Lice jump"**: they crawl from hair to hair.
**"Nits mean active lice"**: empty egg cases stay glued to hair for months.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: The louse lives on the scalp and feeds on blood; itch is an **allergic reaction** to its saliva.

mech.t: Females lay up to 10 eggs a day, cemented to the hair shaft close to the scalp; they hatch in 7–10 days.
mech.caption: Louse and nits (eggs) glued close to the scalp on the hair shaft.

mech.t: Nymphs become adults in about 7–10 days; adults live about 30 days and die within 1–2 days off the head.
Lice feed on blood several times a day; sensitisation to saliva causes **itch after 4–6 weeks** of a first infestation.
Combing wet, conditioned hair with a fine-toothed comb is the most reliable way to find live lice.
mech.caption: Detection combing in sections from the scalp to the ends.

histo: Not relevant; diagnosis is by detection combing and seeing a live louse.

ul: Scalp itch (often absent), tickling, and excoriations — especially **behind the ears and at the nape**.
Live grey-brown lice that move away from light; eggs/nits cemented to the shaft.
Complications: secondary impetigo, occipital lymphadenopathy, eczematisation, sleep disturbance and school stigma.

sections.title: Diagnosis and investigations
blocks: **Only a live louse confirms active infestation (NICE CKS).** Nits alone do not justify treatment.

ul: **Detection combing** with a fine-toothed plastic comb on wet conditioned hair (or dry) is more sensitive than looking alone.
Check **all household members** and treat only those with live lice, **all on the same day**.
Nits stay put; dandruff and hair casts brush or slide off.

sections.title: Management
blocks: Treat **only when a live louse is found**. Choice depends on preference, age, asthma/eczema and previous treatment.

Notes
rows: Conditioner + detection comb days 1, 5, 9 and 13; check day 17
Suitable for everyone including infants, pregnancy, asthma and eczema
Dry hair, leave overnight (check product), wash out; **repeat after 7 days**
Physical insecticide; CKS first-line in pregnancy, breastfeeding, young children, asthma/eczema. Flammable while on hair

blocks.title: Not recommended in the UK
blocks.text: **Permethrin** creme rinses (unsuitable contact time and widespread resistance), shampoos alone, herbal/essential-oil products, electric combs, and “preventive” treatment of people without live lice.

ul: Detection-comb 2–3 days after finishing treatment and again after 7 days.
If live lice persist, check technique then switch to a **different mode of action**.
Oral ivermectin or co-trimoxazole for resistant lice are **specialist/off-label** — refer rather than start them yourself.

blocks.title: Prescribing limits and pitfalls
list: **Not recommended (UK)**: Permethrin creme rinse, shampoos alone, herbal oils, electric combs, ‘preventive’ treatment.
**No exclusion**: No school exclusion, boil-washing or fumigation.

refer.t: Pubic lice on a child’s **eyelashes** → safeguarding pathway.
Infant **under 6 months**: wet combing only; seek advice if it fails.
Extensive secondary infection, severe eczematous scalp, or suspected misdiagnosis.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Infant under 6 months (wet combing only; seek advice if this fails).
Repeated failure despite correct technique.
Extensive secondary infection or severe eczematous scalp.
Pubic lice on a child’s eyelashes → safeguarding pathway.
Suspected misdiagnosis (tinea capitis, psoriasis).
Scalp **excoriations and dermatitis**; secondary bacterial infection (impetigo) and enlarged neck nodes.
Anxiety, stigma and school disruption.
Curable; reinfestation from untreated contacts is common.
Treatment failure is usually due to incorrect use, resistance or reinfestation.

pearls: There is **no school exclusion** and no need to boil-wash bedding or fumigate. Inform school only as local practice.
Asthma/eczema: prefer wet combing or aqueous dimeticone; avoid alcohol-based lotions.
Itch can persist a few days after cure; leftover nits alone do not mean failure.
UK teaching point: course materials that recommend permethrin for head lice are **out of step with CKS**.

quiz.a: A live louse (found by detection combing). Nits alone don’t.
Days 1, 5, 9 and 13, with a check on day 17.
On dry hair, left on (often overnight per product), washed out, repeated after 7 days.

quiz.q: Is permethrin recommended for head lice in the UK?
quiz.a: No: unsuitable contact time and widespread resistance.
